title: Renewed Confirmed-Case Reporting in Health Zones After 21 Days Without a Newly Attributed Case During the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: Implications for Health-Zone Surveillance and Response

analysis.research_question_and_background: During the geographically dispersed 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), 21 days without a newly attributed confirmed case may inform health-zone surveillance and resource-allocation decisions while transmission continues elsewhere. However, the frequency and timing of renewed confirmed-case reporting after this interval have not been quantified.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted among health zones affected by the 2026 BVD outbreak in the DRC. Health zones that completed 21 days without a newly attributed confirmed case by 2 August 2026 entered the cohort.
analysis.methods: The primary data source was the national situation-report series, triangulated with World Health Organization weekly reports. The observed recurrence proportion, incidence per 100 zone-days and Kaplan-Meier time to recurrence were estimated.
analysis.main_results: Seventeen of 51 affected health zones completed the 21-day interval. Ten subsequently reported recurrence and seven were right-censored, giving an observed recurrence proportion of 58.8% (95% exact confidence interval 32.9% to 81.6%). The incidence was 2.83 recurrences per 100 zone-days (95% confidence interval 1.36 to 5.21). The estimated cumulative probability of recurrence was 20.0% by day 7, 41.3% by day 14, 48.7% by day 21 and 56.0% by day 28; median recurrence-free time was 22 days.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Completion of 21 days without a newly attributed confirmed case was frequently followed by reported recurrence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The interval should not be used as a stand-alone trigger for substantial surveillance de-escalation. Decisions should also consider subsequent observation time, nearby case activity, surveillance performance and unresolved laboratory or reporting constraints.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Aggregate reports could not distinguish persistent undetected transmission, reintroduction, delayed confirmation or retrospective attribution. The evidence is moderate as the study is based on aggregated reports and does not account for all potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the frequency and timing of renewed confirmed-case reporting in health zones affected by the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo after 21 days without a newly attributed case. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using national situation reports and WHO weekly reports to estimate recurrence proportion, incidence, and time to recurrence. Seventeen of 51 health zones completed the 21-day interval, with 10 reporting recurrence and 7 being right-censored, resulting in an observed recurrence proportion of 58.8% (95% CI 32.9% to 81.6%) and an incidence of 2.83 recurrences per 100 zone-days (95% CI 1.36 to 5.21). The cumulative probability of recurrence was 20.0% by day 7, 41.3% by day 14, 48.7% by day 21, and 56.0% by day 28, with a median recurrence-free time of 22 days. The authors conclude that the 21-day interval should not be used as a standalone trigger for surveillance de-escalation, as it may not account for ongoing transmission or other factors. The study has moderate evidence strength due to reliance on aggregated reports and potential confounding factors.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these narratives as rooted in prior experiences of corruption, unequal resource distribution, coercive authority, and limited transparency rather than biomedical ignorance alone. analysis.summary_en: This desk-based qualitative synthesis examined why communities doubted the legitimacy of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These narratives were linked to operational challenges including delayed care-seeking, resistance to isolation, and hostility toward responders. The authors argue that trust is not merely a communication outcome but a component of outbreak-control infrastructure, requiring transparent procedures, fair resource use, respectful patient treatment, and community participation. The evidence strength is moderate due to reliance on secondary sources and lack of primary data or quantitative validation.

title: Rapid and portable reverse-transcription quantitative PCR assays for Bundibugyo ebolavirus detection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak highlighted the urgent need for diagnostic tools that can be rapidly deployed in field settings to detect ebolaviruses with high specificity and minimal infrastructure.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study developed and analytically validated multiple reverse-transcription quantitative PCR assay formats targeting BDBV, Zaire ebolavirus, and Sudan ebolavirus without specifying a human or animal cohort or clinical sample source.
analysis.methods: Assays included a BDBV singleplex TaqMan assay, a duplex assay with a human internal control, a four-target multiplex assay for ebolavirus differentiation, and a probe-free SYBR Green assay, all adapted to a portable qPCR instrument with lyophilized reagents.
analysis.main_results: All TaqMan formats achieved a 95% limit of detection of 5 copies per reaction across instruments and reagent types, while the SYBR Green assay achieved a 95% limit of detection of 50 copies per reaction.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the development of rapid, portable, and deployable molecular diagnostics for BDBV and related ebolaviruses to enhance outbreak response and surveillance capabilities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to analytical validation without clinical performance evaluation, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of field testing or patient-derived sample validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed and analytically validated multiple reverse-transcription quantitative PCR assays for detecting Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV), Zaire ebolavirus, and Sudan ebolavirus, including singleplex, duplex, multiplex, and SYBR Green formats. All TaqMan assays achieved a 95% limit of detection of 5 copies per reaction across instruments and reagent types, while the SYBR Green assay achieved 50 copies per reaction. The assays were adapted to a portable qPCR instrument with a reduced runtime of 35 minutes and validated lyophilized reagents to minimize cold-chain dependence. Analytical specificity was confirmed by lack of cross-reactivity among tested ebolavirus species in contrived clinical samples. Protocols were shared in real time via open-access platforms. The study addresses the need for rapid, deployable diagnostics during ebolavirus outbreaks but is limited by the absence of clinical validation and field testing.

analysis.summary_en: This paper presents a qualitative synthesis of burial practices during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The study highlights the importance of family participation and trust in ensuring the legitimacy of safe burial practices. Key findings include the need for culturally sensitive approaches, such as locally recruited teams and ritual substitution, to address community resistance and improve public health outcomes. The paper argues that dignity and infection control are not mutually exclusive but must be balanced through inclusive and respectful practices. However, the evidence does not quantify gender-specific risks, and there is a need for further research on how gendered caregiving influences exposure during outbreaks.

title: Deadbolt Drug Discovery: Locking the Door to Class 1 Viral Entry by Small Molecules.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the development of small-molecule inhibitors targeting Class 1 viral entry proteins, specifically in the context of Ebola viruses and related pathogens. The central question is whether these inhibitors can effectively block viral entry and serve as potential antiviral therapeutics for diseases caused by these viruses.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of recent advances in small-molecule entry inhibitors targeting viruses with Class 1 fusion proteins. It includes studies from the past five years and highlights the mechanisms of action and efficacy of these inhibitors against specific viral targets.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that small-molecule inhibitors targeting Class 1 fusion proteins have shown promise in preventing viral entry, which is a critical early step in infection. These inhibitors are considered attractive candidates for antiviral therapy due to their ability to block the virus before it causes significant damage to host cells.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that while there is agreement on the potential of these inhibitors, the evidence is still limited in terms of long-term efficacy and safety. title: High-Resolution Mapping of Environmental Suitability for Reported Ebola Spillover Events in Uganda to Inform Surveillance and Preparedness.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Uganda experiences recurrent Ebola disease (EBOD) outbreaks, yet national suitability maps often pool virus species or are too coarse for district-level planning.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We aimed to generate species-resolved, 1 km relative environmental suitability surfaces for reported Ebola spillover events in Uganda; quantify the contribution of environmental, anthropogenic, and reservoir-related predictors to modeled suitability; and translate continuous outputs into operational prioritization tiers for district surveillance and preparedness.
analysis.methods: We compiled 71 laboratory-confirmed reported Ebola event localities in Uganda from 2000 to 2023, defined as the most likely documented locality of initial human infection where available, and paired them with 11 minimally collinear predictors.
analysis.main_results: Tuning selected LQHP with β = 1.5 for the pooled model. Under spatial block cross-validation, pooled performance was Test AUC = 0.845 (0.825 to 0.862) and Test Boyce = 0.58 (0.52 to 0.63), with Test OR10 = 0.101 (0.092 to 0.109). The operational threshold was cloglog = 0.084, classifying 25.4% of Uganda as suitable within the modeling framework.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Relative environmental suitability for reported Ebola spillover localities in Uganda is concentrated in compact high-priority belts where elevated modeled suitability overlaps with large resident populations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Tier 1 and Tier 2 areas provide a focused basis for strengthening event-based surveillance, early detection, laboratory referral, infection prevention and control readiness, rapid response capacity, One Health field investigation, and community engagement.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Performance was estimated using fourfold spatial block cross-validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to generate high-resolution environmental suitability maps for reported Ebola spillover events in Uganda, focusing on species-specific models to guide surveillance and preparedness. The researchers compiled 71 laboratory-confirmed event localities from 2000 to 2023 and paired them with 11 minimally collinear predictors. They used MaxEnt models tuned via ENMeval and validated performance using fourfold spatial block cross-validation. The results showed that the pooled model selected LQHP with β = 1.5, achieving a Test AUC of 0.845 and Test Boyce of 0.58. The operational threshold classified 25.4% of Uganda as suitable, with Tier 1 areas covering 5.8% of the land and containing 29% of the population. High-suitability areas were concentrated in specific geographic regions, and species-specific outputs were interpreted as exploratory. The findings suggest that targeted surveillance and preparedness efforts should focus on these high-priority belts to enhance outbreak response capabilities.

title: Dynamics, Optimal Control, and Spillover Risk of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the dynamics of the 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and assess its spillover risk to inform control strategies. The outbreak, with 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths as of 11 August 2026, potentially became the largest Ebola outbreak on record.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A susceptible-exposed-infectious-deceased-recovered (SEIDR) model was developed to evaluate early transmission dynamics, the current epidemic trajectory, and cross-border spillover risk. The model incorporated three categories of interventions: public self-protection, safe burial, and treatment and convalescence.
analysis.methods: The study used International Migrant Stock data and Facebook IP-based mobility data with the Prophet forecasting model to assess spillover risk. Sensitivity analyses across multiple candidate start dates identified 28 March as the optimal start date of sustained transmission.
analysis.main_results: As of 31 July 2026, the basic reproduction number (R0) was 1.83 (95% CI: 1.81-1.84). When 58.12% of the susceptible population adopted protective behaviours, the transmission chain could be effectively interrupted.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that a significant proportion of the population adopting protective measures could interrupt the transmission chain. The study introduced an integrated model combining non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) with Pontryagin's minimum principle (PMP) to derive a time-varying optimal control strategy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted control strategies to mitigate the spread of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak in the DRC and reduce global importation risk. Enhanced entry screening and preparedness are warranted in neighboring countries.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relied on cumulative confirmed case data up to 31 July 2026, which may limit the accuracy of transmission dynamics modeling. The evidence strength is moderate due to the use of abstract-only data and the assumptions inherent in the forecasting model.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), identifying it as potentially the largest Ebola outbreak on record with 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths. Using a susceptible-exposed-infectious-deceased-recovered (SEIDR) model, the researchers assessed transmission dynamics and spillover risk, incorporating interventions such as public self-protection, safe burial, and treatment. The basic reproduction number (R0) was estimated at 1.83 (95% CI: 1.81-1.84), and the model suggested that 58.12% of the susceptible population adopting protective behaviors could interrupt transmission. An optimized control strategy using NSGA-II and Pontryagin's minimum principle was proposed to reduce the epidemic duration by approximately 7 months. The study highlights the importance of enhanced entry screening and preparedness in neighboring countries to mitigate global importation risk. However, the reliance on abstract-only data and assumptions in the forecasting model limits the confidence in the findings, resulting in a moderate evidence strength assessment.

title: A qualitative participatory study on adolescent mental health and well-being in Sierra Leone

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study was needed because adolescents in Sierra Leone face layered crises—civil conflict, the 2014–2016 Ebola virus disease outbreak, and COVID-19—that intensify pre-existing vulnerabilities in mental health, education, and family stability.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A qualitative participatory study was conducted across three districts in Sierra Leone between February and July 2024, recruiting 112 participants including adolescents aged 13 to 19 years, caregivers, teachers, youth leaders, community health workers, counsellors, and child protection actors.
analysis.methods: Data were collected through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, emotion mapping, personal timelines, and guided storytelling, with reflexive thematic analysis applied to interpret the findings.
analysis.main_results: Four themes emerged: landscapes of distress (grief, fear, poverty-related shame, school disruption), gendered and intersecting vulnerabilities (early marriage, sexual violence, differential educational access), coping and resilience (faith, peer solidarity, creative expression, aspiration), and navigating support (trust barriers, stigma, informal networks).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret adolescent mental health in Sierra Leone as shaped by layered, intersecting crises that exceed individual-level coping, highlighting the need for school-based psychosocial support, community-level stigma reduction, and gender-responsive services.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support prioritizing school-based psychosocial support, community stigma reduction, and gender-responsive mental health services to address adolescent distress in post-crisis Sierra Leone.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The qualitative design and purposive sampling limit generalizability, and the absence of quantitative measures or longitudinal follow-up constrains causal inference; evidence strength is assessed as moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative participatory study in Sierra Leone examined how adolescents experience mental health, well-being, coping, schooling, and post-crisis recovery amid layered crises including civil conflict, the 2014–2016 Ebola virus disease outbreak, and COVID-19. Conducted across three districts from February to July 2024 with 112 participants, the study used in-depth interviews, focus groups, emotion mapping, personal timelines, and guided storytelling, analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: distress landscapes, gendered vulnerabilities, coping and resilience, and support navigation. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that intersecting crises overwhelm individual coping, underscoring the need for school-based psychosocial support, community stigma reduction, and gender-responsive services. The qualitative design and purposive sampling limit generalizability, and the absence of quantitative measures constrains causal inference, yielding a moderate evidence strength.
